(
    MAT283 Calculus
    AND CSE400 Fundamentals of Probability in Computing
  )
description: Machine learning is designing and developing algorithms for machines especially computers to showcase a human like behavior i.e., learning from the environment and be adaptive to environmental changes. In doing so they may use the experimental data set or human expertise. Learning is extremely helpful when human expert is missing. Machine learning uses statistics in building the mathematical models and optimize their parameters through learning. This course aims to build the fundamental building blocks of machine learning. The core focus would be on developing algorithms that learn complex patterns from the data and make intelligent decisions.

name: Social Network Analysis
prerequisite:
(
    CSE210 Data Structures and Algorithms
    AND CSE211 Data Structures and Algorithms Lab
  )
description:
Social Network Analysis (SNA) is about analysing networks arising in various 																																					 														        contexts, especially those arising in social contexts: as a result of peopleconnecting with each other on online social networks such as Twitter andFacebook, as well as “who-calls-whom” graph arising out of Telecom networks. However, the techniques for analysing social networks can be extended to other non-social networks as well.
In this course, we will learn about techniques for analysing networks, bothsocial and others, and also learn about how (algorithms) to do this in ascalable manner. Also, we will learn how to visualise some of these largenetworks. And lastly, we will also explore the applications of SNA in variousdomains such as Telecom, Biology, Economics, etc.
We will discuss the following topics:- Graph Theory and Social Networks- Visualizing Social Networks- Game Theory- Network Dynamics- Information Networks and the World Wide Web- Applications of SNA in various domains

name: Computer Vision
prerequisite:
(
    ECE501 Digital Image Processing
    AND CSE100 Fundamentals of Computer Programming
    AND MAT281 Multivariable Calculus
    AND CSE305 Data Structures
  )
description:
Computer vision (CV) is about extracting semantics and descriptions from the images or videos. This helps to analyze and understand the world around us. It allows visual perception in the Artificial Intelligence agent. CV occupies a significant importance in the fields of healthcare, mobility, security, entertainment, and robotics. The major thrust of the course will be to develop models and to put them in practice through algorithms on images and videos. This will translate ideas from theory to practice.
The course is meant to cover recent advances in the domain of computer vision.  The course will gradually meander from low level computer vision to high level concepts. It will introduce tradition CV topics like filters, local image features and texture descriptors, then move to mid-level vision covering visual matching through Hough transform, optical flow. It ends up in high-level vision tasks like segmentation, tracking, classification, detecting objects and person recognition.

name: Introduction to Blockchain: Technologies, Approaches and Applications
prerequisite:
CSE205 Data Structures
  OR
  CSE250 Database Management Systems
description:
Blockchain is considered disruptive and game-changer solution in areas that involve multiple stakeholders, each having complex business processes implemented in unique systems and infrastructure; operating in different administrative and geopolitical boundaries. With cross-organization workflows and complex compliance requirements, industry sectors like Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, International Trade, Insurance, Retail, Supply Chain, Recruitment, Media, Real-estate, and Education etc. can benefit significantly by improved operational efficiency, enhanced security, and transparency offered by blockchain implementation.

However, Blockchain technology practices and research activities are currently in initial phase and evolving continuously with new tools, technologies, approaches and application strategies. In such scenario, it is difficult for students, researchers or practitioners to get right entry into the subject. This course will be instrumental in developing familiarity with theoretical concepts, underlying technology, tools, implementation strategies and current practices.  The course will offer detailed overview of two major technology stacks, along with detailed technical discussion on application and research areas.

name: Applied Data Science
description: This course covers the fundamentals of data science and its relevance in the real-time applications. Students will learn about data acquisition, cleaning, and preprocessing techniques, including web scraping and handling missing data. Exploratory data analysis techniques followed by an introduction to data mining using tree-based and ensemble classifiers will be covered in the course. Students will explore big data technologies like Hadoop and Apache Spark, advanced data visualization, storytelling with data, and time series analysis. The course will be taught through activity-based learning where students apply their skills to real-world data challenges, showcasing their understanding of data exploration, analysis, modeling, and presentation.

name: Deep Learning
prerequisite:
CSE523 Machine Learning
  OR
  CSE641 Computer Vision: Modern Methods and Applications
  OR
  ECE501 Digital Image Processing
  OR
  CSE623 Machine Learning Theory and Practice
description: This deep learning course offers a comprehensive dive into advanced Artificial Intelligence  (AI) techniques. Students will learn about core architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which have applications in spatial data processing like images and videos.  The architectures of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) will provide an understanding of sequence data processing like speech or text. The course also covers optimization methods, deep generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and transformative technologies such as transformers and large language models (LLMs) used in Natural Language Processing (NLP). The curriculum extends into computer vision (CV) and explores hybrid models combining multiple neural architectures for the processing of vision and language together.

name: Network Science: Theory and Applications
description:
Network Science Theory and Applications (NetSci) is about understanding
and analysing networks arising in various contexts, including social,
technological and economic.

In this course, we will learn about techniques for understanding networks
using models.  We will learn about analysing networks, including about how
how to do this in a scalable manner (algorithms). We will also explore the
applications of NetSci in various domains such as Telecom, Biology, Economics,
etc.

We will discuss the following topics:
- Graph Theory and Social Networks
- Mathematics of Networks
- Network Models
- Game Theory
- Network Dynamics
- Information Networks and the World Wide Web
- Strategic Network Formation
- Learning and Networks
- Applications of Network Science in various domains

prerequisite:

    CSE210 Data Structures and Algorithms

    AND STA100 Probability

  (

    AND ENR106 Introduction to Programming: AI Application

  )
description: Welcome to a CSE 623 course on Machine Learning Theory and Practice. It introduces machine learning algorithms in supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. The course helps to develop computational thinking and strengthen programming skills to apply machine learning to problems in diverse domains.

name: MTech CSE Thesis: Implementation Details and Comparative Evaluations
description: The course is designed for M.Tech. CSE students' Master’s thesis who will be working on their project at any external institute (or company) or internally at Ahmedabad University. If the project is external, the student will be assigned a SEAS Faculty member as a co-mentor. In this course, the students will explain the technical details of their implementation, and do comparative evaluation and analysis of their approach with prior art.

name: MTech CSE Thesis: Results and Comprehensive Report
description: The course is designed for M.Tech. CSE students' Master’s thesis who will be working on their project at any external institute (or company) or internally at Ahmedabad University. If the project is external, the student will be assigned a SEAS Faculty member as a co-mentor. In this course, the students will analyse the results, discuss limitations and outline future work. Also, they will compile a comprehensive report and present their research.

name: Fundamentals of Integrated Circuit Devices
description: This course quickly reviews the concepts of Semiconductor Device Electronics and then focuses on the Modern Integrated Circuit Devices. The course begins with review of  Semiconductor Fundamentals, Energy Band Diagrams, Continuity Equation and covers different types of currents in semiconductors. These concepts are applied to PN Junction Diode to discuss PN Junction Electrostatics and I-V Characteristics of Ideal and Non-Ideal PN Junction devices. Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) are studied in details including topics on voltage-current relationships, capacitances, switching properties, small signal models and the design aspects of modern BJTs and HBTs. Metal Oxide Semiconductor (MOS) structure is explored with modern non-ideal effects. MOS Field Effect Transistor (MOSFET) is explored in details including Voltage-Current Characteristics, Scaling of Modern MOSFETS,  Modern MOSFET Structures, Design aspects of Modern MOSFET, Small Signal Model, Introduction to Modern IC Devices like FinFET and MOS Non-volatile Memory structure. The course covers the fundamentals, advance aspects and design aspects of modern semiconductor devices used in Integrated Circuits.

name: Digital CMOS VLSI Design
description:
Introduction to CMOS VLSI Technology, and MOSFET: Introduction to CMOS logic and MOSFET structure; Trends in VLSI industry and scaling; Gate Leakage; Sub-threshold leakage; Solutions: high-k dielectrics, fin based transistors; Power density; Dimensions of interest in planar MOSFET (such as tox, W, L, M1 pitch) and FinFET (such as fin width, fin height, gate-length, fin-extension; fin pitch, gate pitch); (Introduction to use of spice tool; Schematic design, Setting the NMOS parameters, and Dual DC Sweep); Simulation of IV Characteristics of NMOSFET; Regions of operation of MOSCAP; Regions of operation of NMOSFET; NMOSFET IV characteristics; IV equations; Numericals to find Ids; Details of ideal IV characteristics of NMOS and PMOS transistors; Numericals based on the variables and constants in IV equations; Comparison of ideal IV shape with simulated IV shape; Numericals (finding Ids and Vds)

Digital CMOS gates (Design, Analysis, and Simulation): 3D view / layout of Inverter; Concepts of metal layers, poly layer, connectivity, contacts; parasitic resistance and capacitance of metal layers, etc; Mask layers for inverter; Concepts related to top- view (layout), and some basic lambda rules for a transistor; Area and Perimeter for Source/Drain; Concept of current mirror; Standard unit-sized Inverter and its sizing; Schematic design (topology) of standard CMOS gates (NAND2, NOR2); CMOS compound gates (schematic design and transistor sizing); Introduction to input patterns/transitions (needed for pattern dependent delay analysis) Transient simulation of Inverter (in tool spice); Use of PWL voltage source; Use of .MEAS commands and .PARAM; Characterization of: propagation delay (tpdLH and tpdHL), trise, tfall, energy and power; Simulation of VTC of inverter (DC sweep simulation); Measurement of VOH, VOL, VIH, VIL, Noise Margins, inverter's threshold; Use of .MEAS commands for the same; Introduction to high-skew and low-skew inverters; Regions of operations (OFF, LIN, SAT) for NMOS and PMOS within the VTC of inverter; Simulation of VTC for skewed inverters; Simulation of NAND2 gate; Measurement of Input pattern/transition dependent delay; Resistive-load NMOS inverter; Pseudo-NMOS inverter; RC modelling (for estimating approximate delay); Numerical/example for inverter RC equivalent, and estimating approximate delay; Numerical/example for RC equivalent for cascade of gates; Concept of FO4 delay (figure of merit); Pattern-dependent RC delay Analysis (Example based on RC equivalent model for NAND2 gate); Basic concepts related to understanding layouts, Euler diagram (Arc/vertices and traversal; PMOS and NMOS diffusion strip) (Example: Inverter layout; NAND2 layout); Layouts of compound gate, cascade of inverters, tri-state inverter; Concepts of: shared S/D areas in the layout; continuity in diffusion strip vs separate transistors Layout of Compound gate, drawn in Electric VLSI tool; Concepts related to drawing transistor of different sizes (with or without share regions) Checks - Layout vs Schematic (LVS) and DRC (design rule check based on lambda rules); Lambda rules corresponding to all layers were covered (Well, Active, Poly, Contacts, Metal); Example of pattern dependent RC delay analysis (for compound gate); Example of pattern dependent RC delay analysis (for compound gate); Concepts related to Pass- Transistor switch and transmission gate; Design NAND2, NOR2, using pass-transistor logic; Creating layout of standard or compound gate in Electric VLSI tool; Pass-Transistor Logic gates (Design of compound gates, based on Shannon's expansion) Introduction to Logical Effort Methodology for delay analysis; Calculating g (logical effort) and p (parasitic delay) for standard gates, compound gates, and skewed gates; Use of Logical effort method for paths with and without branches; transistor/gate sizing; Concepts related to static and dynamic power dissipation in CMOS gates; Dynamic Logic Circuits: Concepts related to pre-charge phase and evaluate phase; Problems with cascading of such gates (leading to domino logic);
This course has Lecture-Tutorial-Practical-Credit (L-T-P-C) structure = 3-0-2-4, which means 3 hrs lecture per week and 2 hrs of lab per week.
Please check the session plan for the details of the Lecture and Laboratory sessions.

name: Optoelectronic Devices
prerequisite:
(
    EEE400 Analog Circuits
    AND EEE305 Semiconductor Device Electronics
  )
description: This course introduces the fundamentals of optoelectronic materials, light-emitting devices, photodetectors, imaging devices, and optical sensors, with an emphasis on the relationships among material properties, device structures, and performance. It explores the operating principles, characterization and performance parameters of optoelectronic devices and sensors, along with emerging materials, technologies, and applications in avenues such as healthcare, environmental monitoring, displays, etc.

name: Design Verification
description:
UNIT I: Introduction (03 hours)
Need of Testing, Different Roles of Testing, Cost and Yield considerations with reference to Testing
UNIT II: Functional Verification Methods and Tools (08 hours)
Concept, test bench architecture, Verification Language, Simulation tools, Functional and Code Coverage
UNIT III: Formal Verification Methods (04 hours)
Binary Decision Diagram, Equivalence Checking, Assertion based verification, Emulation
UNIT IV: Fault Models (10 hours)
Stuck-at Models, Transistor Short-Open Model, Bridge Fault Models, Single-Stuck-At Models, Fault Equivalence and Fault Dominance
UNIT V: Automatic Test Pattern Generator (10 hours)
Deterministic Test Pattern generation, Basic and Advance Algorithm for test pattern Generation, Types of test pattern sets, ATPG System
UNIT VI: Design-For-Test and Built-In-Self-Test (10 hours)
Introduction, Testability Analysis, Adhoc DFT Methods, Structured DFT Methods, Scan-Chain Based Design, Built-In-Self-Test Design Rules and Logic;  BIST Architecture

name: Printed Electronics Technologies
description: Printed Electronics Technologies introduces materials, processes, device architectures, and design methods used to manufacture electronic functions by printing and additive deposition. The course covers functional inks, flexible and stretchable substrates, contact and digital printing, drying and sintering, multilayer integration, metrology, and reliability. Device modules include printed interconnects, passive components, transistors, physical and electrochemical sensors, wearables, e-textiles, energy devices, and hybrid systems. Students learn to select compatible material-process combinations and evaluate performance, manufacturability, safety, and environmental impact. Sustainable, recyclable, and biodegradable electronics are treated through circular design and life-cycle assessment.

name: MTech Major Project-II
prerequisite:
(
    ECE511 Fundamentals of Integrated Circuit Devices
    AND ECE512 Digital CMOS VLSI Design
    AND ECE514 Electronic Materials and Properties
    AND ECE551 VLSI Sub-system Design
    AND ECE550 Introduction to IC Fabrication Technology
    AND ECE554 Design Verification
  )
description: The M.Tech Major Project, is a research-driven (in case of on-campus thesis) or hands-on project-driven (in case of off-campus industry project) course spread across the Monsoon (ECE610 MTech Major Project-I) and Winter (ECE611 MTech Major Project-II) semesters of the second (final) year of the postgraduate programme. This course provides students with an opportunity to integrate advanced theoretical knowledge, specialized engineering principles, and practical skills acquired throughout their studies to address a complex, real-world engineering challenge or contribute to cutting-edge scientific research. Under the guidance of a faculty supervisor (in case of on-campus thesis) or industry mentor (in case of off-campus industry project), students will independently navigate the entire lifecycle of a research/project work. This includes conducting a rigorous and systematic literature review, identifying critical research gaps, formulating well-defined problem statements, and proposing innovative methodologies or system architectures. Depending on the nature of the research, students will design mathematical models, execute high-fidelity simulations, or build experimental laboratory setups using state-of-the-art software tools and technologies. A heavy emphasis is placed on critical data analysis, result validation against established benchmarks, academic integrity, and plagiarism-free research practices. Beyond the technical implementation, the course aims to hone the students' professional communication skills. Ultimately, students are required to document their methodology and findings in a standard thesis/project report, defend their work before an evaluation committee, and attempt to publish their contributions in reputed journals or conferences.

name: The World of Electrical Engineers
description: The course includes practical exposure related to basic Electrostatics, Electrical circuits, insight into Electronics, Electromagnetics, circuit simulators, introduction to Electrical Machines, Power generation and distribution, history and growth of semiconductors and VLSI technology. Course will me mainly hands-on and field experience based.

name: Hardware Description Language Laboratory
ELECTRICAL CIRCUITS AND NETWORKS
description: This is an in depth course for electrical circuits and networks. It buiids upon the previous course ENR 207 (Electric and magnetic circuits). The topic of transient response will be studied in detail for first order as well as higher order circuits.Detailed study of Laplace transform as applied to electrical circuits will be undertaken. Pole zero concepts and their applications will be introduced

name: Engineering Electromagnetics
description: This course covers the principles of microwave engineering and transmission lines with emphasis on electromagnetic wave propagation, impedance matching, waveguides, and microwave components. Students will learn theoretical foundations along with laboratory exposure to measurements and analysis using modern tools and equipment.

name: Control Systems Engineering
prerequisite:
(
    EEE203 Signals and Systems
    AND ENR213 Control Engineering Fundamentals
  )

name: Semiconductor Device Electronics
prerequisite:
EEE301 ELECTRICAL CIRCUITS AND NETWORKS
  OR
  EEE201 Fields and Waves
  OR
  ENR207 Electric and Magnetic circuits
description: This course focuses on the concepts of Semiconductor Device Electronics. The course begins with Semiconductor Fundamentals, Energy Band Diagrams, Carrier Mobility and Scattering, Carrier Distribution, Equilibrium Carrier Concentration, and Continuity Equation. These concepts are applied to PN Junction Diode to discuss PN Junction Electrostatics, Ideal I-V Characteristics, and Deviation from Ideal Characteristics. The course extends the understanding of the PN junction diode to Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT) and covers BJT Static Characteristics, Ideal Transistor Analysis and Deviation from Ideal Characteristics. The Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (MOS) structure is studied with the focus on MOS Capacitor Energy Band Diagrams, Electrostatics, Major Regions of Operation, and Non-idealities in MOS structure. The learning is then extended to MOS Field Effect Transistor (MOSFET) to study qualitative theory of MOSFET Operation, Derivation of ideal I-V Characteristics, Deviation from ideal characteristics and Introduction to the  MOSFET Scaling. Selected Modern Aspects of MOSFET are covered towards the end of the course.

name: Power Systems

(
    EEE301 ELECTRICAL CIRCUITS AND NETWORKS
    AND EEE401 Electromechanics and electrical machines
  )

name: Analog and Digital Communications
prerequisite:
(

    AND EEE203 Signals and Systems
  )

name: Product Dissection and Realization
description: This course imparts knowledge on the study of products with emphasis on generating bill of materials, part naming and numbering, their materials of construction and processes of manufacture. Aspects of mechanical, electrical, electronics, and civil engineering, amongst others, and design and ergonomics are experienced. Students practice a variety of hands-on manufacturing operations, followed by making of a multi-part, multi-process components to realize a product. Processes of manufacture include, but are not limited to machining, 3D printing, joining and welding, weaving, casting, finishing and painting, using materials, such as, mild steel, aluminium, wood, polymeric materials, concrete mixes, and fabrics, amongst others.

name: Introduction to Programming: AI Application
description: The course begins with logical problem solving exercises and then introduces the students to the world of programming using Python and C. The course includes rigorous lab exercises with scenario-based problem-solving questions and classical computer science puzzles. Lab exercises include a range of practical activities, such as completing given code, debugging, designing alternative solutions, and enhancing existing code for different challenges. Students are expected to finish these lab exercises as a requirement of the course. The course also introduces C language to the students for their future courses. This is a beginner-level computer programming course designed for engineering students.

name: Digital Electronics and Microprocessors
description:
The course has two parts. One part centers around a computer board which is interfaced to input and output devices and explores the use of Analog to Digital converters and Digital to analog converters and the operations through a computer program.
The second part involves the study of architecture of microprocessors. The functions of - data and address bus , program counter, stack pointers , registers and arithmetic logic units  and control unit will be studied. The distinction between serial and parallel I/O operations will be explored. The concept of interrupts will be studied. Introduction to assembly language programs will be given  and sample programs will be studied .
Since computerized measurement and control is now present in all the branches of Engineering this foundation for the same will be highly useful for students of all the Engineering disciplines

name: Materials and the Engineering World
description: Starting with history, the course will look at the evolution of materials, their applications, and processing using the compendium Cambridge Engineering Selector as a guide. Physical, chemical and biological properties will be discussed. These properties will be connected with the science of material structure, such as, crystals and grains, at different length scales. Standards of materials designation will be introduced, as also how these materials are available in the market. Hands-on laboratory work will give experience of measuring material properties, and structure of materials. Engineering uses and environmental aspects of the products will be integrated into the course.

name: Linear Algebra Laboratory
description: In this beginner level course, concepts of linear algebra are covered via MatLab/SciLab based practice. Topics include: fundamentals of vectors and vector space, matrices and its operations: addition, subtraction, multiplications, division, matrix types. Systems of linear equations. Gauss elimination and Gauss-Jordan methods. Linear dependence and rank of a matrix. Determinant. Cramer’s rule.  Matrix inverse, diagonalization, orthogonalization, LU factorization. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors. These concepts will be illustrated with applications, such as, electric circuits, piped fluid systems/piping network, graphical projections such as planes, lines and rotations, stress analysis, heat transfer, traffic flow, structures, and others.

name: Chemistry in the Engineering World
description: This course introduces chemistry in the context of engineering applications whose details are taught in later courses. Chemistry aspects and basics related to a variety of applications, such as, fuels, fertilizers, water, displays, (OLED), polymers, energy (battery, fuel cells), beverages, nutrition, semi-conductors, metals and alloys, oils, detergents, paints, pollutants, foods, and medicines, amongst others. When studying these topics, students will be trained on use of state-of-the-art instruments applicable to the sector. Implications of chemistry on technological advances will be illustrated.

name: Engineering Visualization and Drawing
description: This course develops the ability to think and communicate pictorially. Concepts of perspectives, orthogonal projections, sectional views, and assembly drawings will be introduced. Free-hand sketching, and making drawings with graphics and CAD software will be extensively practiced. Skills on making animations using animation and CAD software will be imparted. Methods of dimensioning and use of standard symbols in mechanical, electrical, architectural, and process plants of will be introduced. AR/VR tools will be used to augment visualization. The importance of CAD in product design will be introduced via small projects.

name: Sensors, Instruments and Experimentation
description: This course gives knowledge and hands-on skills about sensors, instrumentations, and their interfacing with computers. Basics of uncertainty analysis are introduced and practised in experiments. Laboratory exercises involve sensor and instrument construction and principles of operation along with specifications/data sheets of manufacturers. Hands-on exercises include installation, calibration, operation, and interfacing with computers/DAS. A variety of instruments and sensors for physical quantities will be considered, such as, temperature, pressure, force, torque, strain, displacement, velocity, acceleration, voltage, current, flow rate, illumination, sound level, etc. Phases of experimentation will be introduced and students will experience these when executing a project experiment.

name: Engineering Thermodynamics
description: This course builds up on the concepts of continuum and balance laws taught in continuum mechanics course, with classical thermodynamics treatment of the First and Second laws, irreversibility and availability, and behaviour of a pure substance and equations of state (and online data). Both control mass and control volume approaches will be considered. Applications of these concepts in energy conversion, particularly power and refrigeration cycles, will be discussed. Energy sources and their uses, and societal and environmental impacts will be discussed.

name: Mechanics of Rigid Bodies
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles of modelling and analysis of a rigid body and rigid multi-body mechanical system. The course emphasizes problem-solving and the students develop critical thinking skills and proficiency in analysis and use of computational tools, preparing them to address real-world engineering challenges in mechanical systems. Key topics include kinematics of a rigid body and rigid multi-body systems, degrees of freedom, force and moments, free-body diagrams, deriving equations of motion using Newton’s laws and Euler’s equation, and energy-based methods, motion analysis and visualization including numerical solutions of equations of motion.

name: Continuum Mechanics
description: This course lays foundation for fundamental theories of continuum mechanics with applications to various disciplines. After defining material and spatial coordinate systems, definitions of various properties of a continuum field are developed. Displacement gradients, strain and stress tensors are defined and explained with associated theories, such as, Hooke’s law for elasticity and plasticity. Yield criteria and plasticity will be covered with practical applications. Balance principles for mass, momentum and energy are discussed with applications. Constitutive equations for different types of materials, including solids, fluids, such as, viscous fluids, Newtonian fluids, plastics, etc. are introduced, along with practical applications from various fields.

name: Statistics for Engineers
prerequisite:
CSD102 Data Science
  OR
  CSD105 Introduction to Data Science
description: Statistics has applications in several aspects of engineering, such as, data interpretation, uncertainty analysis in experiments, quality control, machine learning, and simulations of networks amongst others. Topics include fundamentals of linear and introduction to multivariable regression, hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, design of experiments, and simulation. Applications will be drawn from engineering experiments, quality control, sampling, numerical integration, and traffic analysis in data networks. The exercises will require use of Python or any other programming language.

name: Design, Innovation and Making
description: Students work in teams that start with customer needs, societal relevance, and problem identification resulting in a project proposal. The second phase, includes development of concept deigns, evaluation of alternative designs, and concept design finalization. Various design techniques, e.g. TRIZ, Poka Yoke, FMEA, etc. and materials selection using CES are used to prepare engineering drawings resulting in a complete engineering design including Bill of Materials (BoM). To realize the design, techniques of DFM, DFA, are applied and manufacturing drawings are prepared. After making or buying the components, the assembly is carried out to realize the proof-of-concept. After testing, the products are displayed in an expo. Finally, manuals are prepared, and recyclability aspects are addressed.

name: Engineering Costing
prerequisite:
ENR105 Product Dissection and Realization
  OR
  ENR215 Design, Innovation and Making
description: This course will introduce various methods of costing for a variety of engineering industries and services, such as, various types of manufacturing, software development and maintenance, utilities (electricity, gas, sewage, water, etc.), and spectrum, amongst others. Methods for New Product Development (NPD), batch and mass manufacture will be discussed. Costing aspects of supply chains will be introduced. The concepts will be extensively illustrated with real/live applications from a variety of industries (light and heavy manufacturing - mechanical, electronics, chemical, etc.), power generation and grid management, software development and maintenance, and transportation, etc. Costs associated with NPD, safety practices and environmental compliance shall be introduced.

name: Introduction to Composites
description: This course is focused on introducing composite materials, a basic understanding of raw materials, and the manufacturing process. This course will cover the micro and macro mechanics of lamina/ply. Macro mechanics of laminate will also be discussed, highlighting stacking sequence and calculation of laminate stiffness matrix based on stacking sequence. This will also cover virtual testing (using ANSYS) of composite laminates subjected to various loading conditions like tensile, bending, impact, and a combination of two or more loads. Virtual tests will follow ASTM standards and industrial problems.

name: Technical Communication
prerequisite:
COM102 Advanced Writing
  OR
  COM101 Effective Reading and Comprehension Skills
description: Engineering graduates have to frequently prepare reports and make presentations. Ability at communication, in general, and technical communication, in particular, is an essential requirement in any organization. This course will be a first exposure to professional practices in technical writing which would include preparation of reports, proposals, poster presentations, oral presentations, and popular writing, amongst others. This skill will be put in practice during project and laboratory work.

name: Mechatronics and Robotics
prerequisite:
(
    ENR213 Control Engineering Fundamentals
    AND ENR312 Control Engineering Laboratory
  )
description: This course provides third-year mechanical engineering students with a comprehensive introduction to the synergistic field of mechatronics and robotics. It covers the fundamental building blocks of intelligent systems, including sensors, actuators, and methods for signal conditioning, data acquisition, programmable logic controllers, pneumatics and machine vision. Weekly lab sessions and a team design project lead students through prototyping, debugging, testing and performance evaluation. The course prepares students to design, implement and validate affordable mechatronic and robotic solutions aligned to manufacturing and service applications.

Engineering Project

name: Advances in Complex Networks
description: Advances in Complex Networks will be based on the latest research and developments in complex networks, as well as their applications to various areas, including both natural and technological networks. In particular, the course will be comprised of the following topics: (i) fundamental concepts of graph theory, (ii) understanding the formulation and applications of various complex network-based metrics, (iii) various complex network models and their characteristics, (iv) graph signal processing on complex networks, and (v) study of various real-world complex networks, which include communication networks (wired and wireless), transportation networks (road, rail, and air), supply chain management networks, education networks, social networks, ecological networks, biological networks, economic networks, and healthcare-allied networks, to name a few. In addition, the students must complete a research project (solo or group activity) as part of the course.

name: Process Integration: Heat Recovery, Pinch Technology, and Network Optimization
prerequisite:
ENR208 Engineering Thermodynamics
  OR
  CHE301 Heat Transfer
  OR
  ENR311 Heat Transfer and Applications
description: This course provides an in-depth understanding of the principles and applications of process integration for improving energy efficiency in industrial systems. It focuses on heat recovery, pinch analysis, energy targeting, and heat exchanger network (HEN) design and optimization. Students will learn how to systematically extract process data, construct composite and grand composite curves, identify pinch points, and develop energy-efficient process and utility networks. The course integrates theoretical concepts with practical design and simulation exercises using software tools such as Aspen Energy Analyzer.

name: Biochemical process design for environmental systems
description: This course covers principles and design of biological wastewater treatment systems, including wastewater characterization, reaction kinetics, biokinetic parameters, suspended and attached growth processes, anaerobic treatment, sludge digestion, nutrient removal, wastewater reclamation, reuse, and effluent disposal with emphasis on sustainable environmental engineering applications. The course also provides limited coverage of biological soil remediation and biologically mediated solid waste management.

name: SEAS Seminar Series
description: None

name: The World of a Mechanical Engineer
description: This course gives a broad overview of how mechanical engineering manifests in applications ranging from energy, transport, health care, agriculture, energy sources, textiles, construction, etc. Starting from a systems approach, exposure will be given to functioning, and functioning of each equipment in the system. Instructions will be imparted using equipment, models, animations, simulations and engineering drawings. The impact of technologies on environment, health and on society will be brought out.

name: Thermal Energy Systems
description: Thermal Energy Systems course deals with the study of heat/power producing/consuming machines. It covers steam cycle, steam turbine, gas turbine, compressors and steam generators. It also covers the relevant cycle and combined cycle based power plant study. These machines are critical parts of the current power generating units.

name: Energy Systems and Sustainability Laboratory
description: This course builds up on concepts and device level analysis of energy conversion systems, based on thermodynamics fundamentals. System level analysis, basics and application based, of power systems, combined cycle power plants, co- and tri-generation cycles will be introduced and this will be connected with primary energy sources utilization. Analysis of refrigeration cycles, Vapor Compression Refrigeration (VCR) and Vapor Absorption Refrigeration (VAM) will be introduced. Fuel cell and electrolyser analysis and their engineering implications will be covered. Integration of these systems with renewables (solar, waste-to-heat, etc.) will be explored. The work will be hands-on in project mode. Issues of sustainability, carbon footprint, energy resources utilization, and societal issues will be built into the exercises

name: Mechanics of solids and designing with materials
prerequisite:
ENR203 Material Science and Engineering
  OR
  ENR108 Materials and the Engineering World
  OR
  ENR209 Mechanics of Rigid Bodies
  OR
  ENR210 Continuum Mechanics
description: This course imparts the knowledge of basics of solid mechanics and their application in the context of designing machines. It integrates theoretical concepts with practical insights, emphasizing the interdisciplinary nature of these subjects. Students will delve into the mechanics of materials, and structural analysis thereby developing the skills necessary for innovative and efficient machine design. Use of CAD and FEM packages will be integrated into product design.

name: Mechanics of Machines, Vibrations and Structures
description: This course focuses on machines, mechanisms and their kinematics and dynamics. The modelling of the motion of components in a mechanism is discussed with kinematic diagrams and inversions, degrees of freedom, velocity and acceleration analysis using CAD tools, for mechanisms, such as, cam, gear trains, flywheels, engine mechanism, robot mechanisms, etc. Free and forced vibration of single degree of freedom systems is covered. Laboratory work will be hands-on in assembling and using various mechanisms and making measurements using sensors, exercises on balancing, and vibration analysis.

name: Materials and Manufacturing Processes Laboratory
prerequisite:
ENR105 Product Dissection and Realization
  OR
  ENR106 Introduction to Programming: AI Application
  OR
  ENR108 Materials and the Engineering World
description: This course builds a practical understanding of the concepts of manufacturing processes and their selection, and use for a given type of material. It enables students to try, fail, and succeed in making a component (or entire product) by manufacturing it using different materials but the same process, and/or by manufacturing it using the same material but different processes. The students will begin by learning to operate various manufacturing tools for different materials. They will learn to make parts from the manufacturing drawings and then inspect the part for geometric dimensions and tolerances. The variables in manufacturing processes, in particular, the experiment matrix of combination of material options (metals, polymers, woods, composites, ceramics, glass) and manufacturing process options (turning, milling, drilling, laser machining, welding, casting, moulding, forming) will be experimented with and comprehended. In subsequent weeks, automation in manufacturing, computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM) systems, and competitive aspects of product design and manufacturing will be delivered. Group project work will begin from the fourth week, where students will build a component (or an entire product), or an experimentation setup, or a machine. The students will draw conclusions in aspects of design, assembly, dimensions, materials, manufacturing processes, and performance.

name: Additive Manufacturing
prerequisite:
ENR105 Product Dissection and Realization
  OR
  ENR106 Introduction to Programming: AI Application
  OR
  ENR108 Materials and the Engineering World
description: This course will establish a comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary trajectory of manufacturing, progressing from conventional methodologies to advanced, regenerative techniques such as Additive Manufacturing (AM). The fundamentals of the main AM types through integrated theory and practice will be discussed. In addition, future trends and research frontiers within these developing processes will be explored. Students will engage in hands-on projects to apply their learnings, focusing on optimizing process capability for specific applications in medical, space, defense, robotics, automotive, energy, and jewellery etc.

name: Product Engineering Case Studies
prerequisite:
MEC307 Mechanics of solids and designing with materials
  OR
  MEC308 Mechanics of Machines, Vibrations and Structures
  OR
  ENR310 Fluid Mechanics and Convective Heat Transfer
  OR
  ENR311 Heat Transfer and Applications
description: All engineered products encompass several subjects of engineering which are taught in respective courses. A synthesis of various subjects is brought out via case studies of engineered products from a mechanical engineering perspective. Beginning with a systems level approach, the functionalities will be identified. A component-wise study of each system will follow including their inter-operability. Aspects of stress analysis, fluid flow, heat transfer, dynamics, etc. will be analysed using CAD/CAE packages for components and systems. Materials selection and manufacturing aspects for components will be explored. Product life cycle analysis, including in-use deterioration, environmental impact footprint and recycling will be carried out, as also regulatory compliances. Two products will be chosen from those in wide use, e.g., pumps, IC engines, aeroengines, tractors, motors, consumer goods, medical devices, machine tools, etc.; two products will be considered in the course.

name: Introduction to General Relativity
description:
In all academic disciplines other than General Relativity, space and time are believed to be merely the passive medium in which everything else takes place. In General Relativity, the stage itself becomes one of the major players in the drama! In the past hundred years, not only have these counter-intuitive ideas been experimentally verified, they have also shaped our thinking about some of the most fundamental questions about the nature of reality.

A firm grounding in General Relativity is absolutely necessary to understand the current exciting advancements in various fields such as Gravitational Waves, Black Hole Physics, Relativistic Astrophysics, Cosmology, Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime, extra dimensions, Quantum Gravity etc. Moreover, various ideas in modern theoretical physics (e.g. gauge-gravity duality) also connect the physics of General Relativity (i.e. physics in curved spacetime) with the physics of strongly coupled quantum systems (such as the kind of systems conventionally studied in condensed matter physics).

This is an entry level course into the exciting world of General Relativity.

name: Democracy and Justice
description: It may be argued that democracy has emerged as the most desirable, if not the most successful, form of government in the contemporary world. Regardless of whether we like a particular democracy or not, arguments about what is the most legitimate and just form of rule point towards democracy. Why is democracy seen as the most just form of rule? How did such a situation come about historically? Is there evidence to show that, all things considered, democracies are indeed the most just form of government known to us?  Are there specific civic virtues that help democracies flourish? Is there a particular way in which agreement, dissent, cooperation, and conversation between different groups and individuals in a democratic society is to be carried out? Would democracy be a necessary component of a just system of government? And would social justice be a necessary component of democratic government?  These are some of the questions that this course will tackle. The entire course is built on two central ideas about democracy: a) how best to safeguard against arbitrary exercise of state power, and b) how best cultivate the virtue of democratic conversation. The course is divided into four taught modules and a fifth project module. Each of the four modules are built around a normative statement, which is supposed to provoke and organise the discussions within that module. The four normative statements are: Module 1: "Democracy is the most just form of government" Module 2: "Rights take precedence over popular will" Module 3:  "Inequality is antithetical to democracy”

name: Environment and Climate Change
description: Since time immemorial, human activities have significantly impacted the nature of our planet. Issues such as depleting resources, climate extremes, land degradation, food insecurity, unsustainable consumption and unequal access to resources, pollution, ecosystem degradation and extinction of species have posed challenges of sustainability that span spatial and temporal scales. However, in the recent past, efforts related to conservation and sustainability have also increased manifold, paving the way for a slightly hopeful future. On the crossroads of these vectors, multiple questions such as: what are the sustainability challenges facing humanity? How do we measure environmental footprints? How do we assess uncertainties and risks? Who bears the burden of costs and risks? Can we make our consumption behavior sustainable? How do we create, replicate and upscale innovative ideas? How do we evolve a just governance system to share costs and benefits equitably?, etc. need to be addressed and answered. The millennials must be equipped to comprehend and answer these questions in a meaningful and an engaging manner. This course, through an integration of diverse domains - materials, data science, biology and life, behaviour, communication, and constitution and civilization, will expose students to 1. appreciate and develop an integrated understanding of these issues and their interactions, 2.

name: Water
description: The two extreme points from where we look at water could be "Water is life, and clean water means health" - Audrey Hepburn, or an extremely scary angle e.g., "World War III will be fought over water"– Special Broadcasting Service (Aug 17, 2017). Both highlight the urgency for us to act - as citizens and as scientists. However, how much do we think of water? How much do we know of this resource apart from what we have read in our school textbooks? Is the water crisis real? Are we taking the right decisions today to secure a better future for the coming generations? How can I, as an individual and as a community participate in the process? Also, as the driver for all forms of life on earth, water is an excellent solvent, however, this excellent solvent’s characteristic, when combined with its flow, makes it a potent carrier of pollutants and pathogenic microorganisms that are often harmful to health. So, what makes water safe to consume and use for many other purposes? Is the water in surface and groundwater bodies in the Ahmedabad area safe for all forms of life? Is it potable? This course will turn students into aware citizens of the country by enabling them to ask relevant questions around the subject of water.

name: An Introduction to Infectious Disease Modelling
description:
This course covers the theory and practice of mathematical modeling in the epidemiology of infectious diseases. It provides students with the tools to understand how infections spread, how interventions influence epidemic trends, and how models can help with public health decisions. Starting with the basics of transmission dynamics, students will learn how to create, analyze, and simulate compartmental models like the SI, SIS, and SIR frameworks. More complex topics will be introduced, including diseases with long incubation periods, vector-borne transmission, and models with seasonality, using case studies of diseases such as tuberculosis, measles, dengue, influenza, COVID-19, and HIV.

A key focus is on the reproduction number, force of infection, and epidemic thresholds, along with methods for estimating these figures from data. The course highlights model building as a process that consists of: (a) turning biological questions into mathematical frameworks, (b) examining model behavior, (c) calibrating against real-world data, and (d) evaluating the effects of interventions like vaccination, quarantine, or vector control.

Students will gain practical experience through R-based sessions that include simulation, model fitting, and inference. By the end of the course, participants will be able to critically assess infectious disease models in scientific literature and create comprehensive models to address research and policy questions.

name: Study design and proposal writing for population based research
description: This course focuses on designing population-based research studies and proposal development. It covers a wide range of topics from formulating research questions that stem from societal problems, conducting literature reviews to understand gaps, and designing different types of observational studies and intervention studies. Students will alongside write sections of a research proposal.

name: Conducting Population-Based Research
description: This course offers hands-on training in applying epidemiological principles to conduct population-based research, encompassing questionnaire design, developing data collection tools, ethical considerations, sampling in the field setting, study participant recruitment and retention, interviewing, clinical assessment techniques, research team and field data management.

name: Epidemiological Data Analysis
description: This course introduces students to advanced statistical methods and data analysis techniques in epidemiology. It covers a range of topics from basic descriptive statistics to complex models. The course includes practical applications and projects that use real-world data to solve epidemiological problems.

name: Deep Learning Foundations for Healthcare
prerequisite:
CSE517 Python Programming
  OR
  EPI706 Data Science for Health
  OR
  CSE623 Machine Learning Theory and Practice
  OR
  CSE523 Machine Learning
  OR
  CSE602 Deep Learning
  OR
  CSE624 AI for Health
description: This course introduces foundational deep learning methods for healthcare data, with an emphasis on understanding how deep neural networks learn, how different model structures represent different kinds of health data, and how to train and evaluate models responsibly. The course focuses on deep neural networks, optimization, representation learning and embeddings, convolution as a reusable building block, recurrent models, attention, autoencoders, and healthcare-specific model evaluation and generalization.
